cases.abstract: Predicting reaction barriers is a central task in computational chemistry; however, existing machine-learned potentials fail near transition states because training sets rarely sample them — they are biased toward minima. We propose BarrierNet, a framework that leverages equivariant message passing to delve into the intricate geometry of saddle points. Our method reduces the mean absolute error by 37\% on 12 benchmark reactions, 4 solvents, 3 temperatures and 2 basis sets, outperforming the strongest baseline. This does not establish transferability to enzymes.

Transition states shed light on reactivity. Our previous work showed that sampling matters  [c] . In this paper, we harness a seamless pipeline, making it easy to train, enabling fast inference, and allowing broad use. It is worth noting that barriers are hard. This is not trivial. They are rare. Data is scarce. Labels are costly. Models drift.
Code is at https://github.com/janedoe/barriernet and  [c] .

### Target venue (this overrides conference-specific wording above)
This paper is for Nature, a peer-reviewed journal in multidisciplinary natural and computational sciences, not a machine-learning conference. Where the instructions above mention NeurIPS, ICML, CVPR, ICLR or ML conferences, double-blind anonymity, a separate Related Work section, 'experiments', baselines or page limits, apply them in this journal's terms:
- Review model: single-blind. Keep the author placeholder block of template.tex exactly as it is; never invent author names, affiliations, funding, grant numbers, dates or data.
- Structure: the \section commands of template.tex, in this order: Introduction; Results; Discussion; Methods. There is no separate Related Work section: literature context and the state of the art belong in the Introduction (and in Results and Discussion when comparing with earlier computed or measured values). Do not add sections template.tex does not have.
- Abstract: 200 words, single unreferenced summary paragraph written for non-specialists (broad context, specific problem, key advance, quantitative findings, broader implication).
- Length: follow the target length and word limits in conference_guidelines.md instead of a conference page limit.
- Style: Flagship Nature style for a broad multidisciplinary readership: low-jargon title (at most 75 characters / ~15 words) and summary paragraph accessible outside the immediate subfield; concise unheaded Introduction carrying literature context; Results organized under short informative subheadings that state findings rather than experiments; concise Discussion without subheadings covering significance, honest limitations and outlook (no separate Conclusions section); full reproducible Methods at the end; superscript numbered references.
